$comment: PERF-ADOPTION §2e (Wave 3 #19), bb's bundle-budget.json taken in shape.
Gates the boot payload: the entry chunk plus its static-import closure,
which is what WebKitGTK parses and compiles before Houston paints. Checked by
scripts/check-bundle-budget.mjs against the bundle-stats.json the build
emits; wired after Build in ci.yml's ui job.
maxBootBytes is a ratchet ~3% above the measured payload (756,406 bytes
minified, one boot chunk). Houston loads from the local filesystem, so
bb's download motivation does not transfer — the parse-and-compile cost
does. Lower it when a change wins headroom; raising it needs a reason in
the commit. No brotli number: nothing compresses the asset protocol's
reads.
The ratchet is only a ratchet if it is re-cut when headroom is won: it
sat at 1,586,571 against a 1,040,739-byte payload — 35% of silent
regression room — because deleting the xterm stack lowered the payload
and nothing lowered the number after it.
forbiddenBootPackages is the more important half — set from the same
measurement: these are exactly the heavy families that are OFF the boot
path today, each kept off by a single dynamic import() that one careless
static import (often via a barrel re-export, which type checking cannot
catch) would undo. The markdown pipeline (react-markdown + rehype/remark
+ micromark + parse5) is gated behind components/markdownPipeline.tsx;
the CodeMirror language modes load through @codemirror/language-data's
own dynamic imports; @tauri-apps/api stays lazy by design — BootstrapGate
and watchdog.ts import it dynamically so the renderer can boot (and the
watchdog can report) before the IPC bridge exists. A `prefix*` entry
matches the whole family.
forbiddenBootPaths is the same gate for code Houston owns instead of installs
(GHOSTTY-CHARTER.md §8 criterion 3 found the gap: `packages` only ever
names things under node_modules/, so an app-local module could never be
protected by name — only by maxBootBytes' byte ratchet, which reports a
size, not a cause). Paths are relative to `ui/`, as recorded in each
chunk's `appModules`; a trailing `/` is a directory rule, `*` a prefix,
anything else an exact file. The ghostty entry keeps the tier-3 terminal
engine (~630 KB of .wasm plus its JS) behind the one `import()` in
TerminalPane's mount effect. Phase C made that engine the default and
Phase E deleted the alternative, so this rule now protects the boot path
from the ONLY engine there is — more load-bearing, not less: boot must
still not pay for the wasm before a pane asks for it.
`pane/ghosttyTerminal.ts` is deliberately NOT listed: it is the facade,
imports only the engine's types (erased at compile time), and is on the
boot path on purpose.
`backdrop/` is the same rule for the custom background, in two layers: the
dither pass and its engine sit behind the one cached `import()` in the
`backdrop/index.ts` facade, and the facade, `source.ts` and `CustomBackdrop`
itself sit behind the one `lazy()` in `backdrop/BackdropMount.tsx`. The mount
is deliberately NOT listed: it is a mode check and nothing else, and it must
be on the boot path to make that check at first paint. A launch on the Solid
default therefore pays for the check, and for nothing under it.
Settings (with its `settings/` sections), the Changes diff surface and the
Skills library are the same rule for three whole surfaces no launch opens:
each is behind one `lazy()`, and each one's type-only imports elsewhere
stay static because types cost no bytes. Naming them here is what makes a
careless `import { SettingsView }` fail with a cause instead of only
nudging the byte ratchet. The SSH modal, the file browser and two Agents
tabs joined them on the same reasoning.
`AgentMemory.tsx` and `BrowserPane.tsx` were the last two holdouts, and
for the same reason: each exported a non-component value App.tsx imports
(`memoryEntryCount`, `tabsStorageKey`), and a value import pins a module
to the boot path however its component is loaded. Both helpers now live in
modules of their own — `agents/memoryEntries.ts` and `browserTabsKey.ts`,
the same shape as `editor/bufferStore.ts` — so the surfaces could go
behind `lazy()` and are named below. Those two helper modules are pure
text/string work with no React and belong on the boot path.
Phase E also retired the `@xterm/addon-webgl` entry with the xterm stack
itself — a forbidden-package rule for an uninstalled package gates
nothing, and the byte ratchet below dropped by the whole xterm payload
in the same commit.
The tag registry manager joined forbiddenBootPaths on the same reasoning:
the chips in tags.tsx render on every sidebar row and belong on the boot
path, while the manager is a surface no launch opens. Splitting it out
gave back 6,196 of the 8,120 bytes v100 session tags added; the rest is
the chips, the editor and the registry wiring, none of which a launch can
avoid. Re-cut here against the new measurement (780,862 bytes, one boot
chunk) at the same ~3% the number has always carried.
`tagEditing.tsx` is the rest of that split, made when the quick editor
grew a hand-over to the manager and pushed the payload past the ceiling:
the name/colour editor and its palette are no more a launch path than the
manager is, and both lazy surfaces now import them from there. tags.tsx is
what is left — the chips a sidebar row actually renders.
